title: PUCT Project 58000, rulemaking to update ERCOT transmission cost recovery, comment deadline reached

title: Abbott orders audit of data centers in the ERCOT interconnection queue, pausing approvals
summary: Governor Greg Abbott directed the Public Utility Commission of Texas and ERCOT to audit data center projects seeking connection to the ERCOT grid, and said projects that fail should be denied connection. ERCOT paused its batch zero review the same day. The order's duration and its pass or fail criteria were not stated when it was announced.

decider.name: Office of the Governor of Texas

key_dates.note: Governor announced the audit and the pause on approvals

public_access.how: A governor's directive letter is not a proceeding and takes no public comment. The place where the public can act on the same subject is the PUCT, whose Large Load Demand Management Service rulemaking is open for comment under control number 58482 until September 4th, 2026.

claims.source_title: The Texas Tribune, quoting a written statement by Governor Greg Abbott

claims.source_title: The Texas Tribune, Data center approvals in Texas halted until audits completed

claims.verbatim_quote: It is unclear how long the audit will take
claims.source_title: The Texas Tribune, Data center approvals in Texas halted until audits completed

notes_for_editor: SOURCING CAVEAT, read before publishing. The primary document is the governor's directive letter to PUCT Chairman Thomas Gleeson and ERCOT CEO Pablo Vegas. gov.texas.gov DISALLOWS ClaudeBot in robots.txt, so this item is sourced entirely to journalism that quotes the document, exactly as instructed. The letter's own URL, for a human to open directly, is https://gov.texas.gov/uploads/files/press/Thomas_Gleeson_Pablo_Vegas_Data_Centers_Directive_Letter_to_PUC_ERCOT_FINAL.pdf recovered from a link inside a press release, not by crawling. Every claim here is now taken from the ENACTED TEXT in the Utilities Code at tcss.legis.texas.gov, an allowed host and the better primary source anyway. No recurring collector should poll BillLookup. Two facts a human can get from Texas Legislature Online by hand if the docket wants them: SB 6 cleared Senate Business and Commerce and House State Affairs with no recorded no vote, and its authors were King and Schwertner. NEGATIVE FINDING, and it corrects the brief this research was given: the widely repeated claim that SB 6 sets a DECEMBER 31ST, 2026 STATUTORY DEADLINE for the PUC to amend four coincident peak transmission cost allocation IS NOT SUPPORTED by anything retrieved. title: TRAIGA in force as Business and Commerce Code Chapter 552, enforceable only by the Attorney General
summary: The Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act took effect on January 1st, 2026 as Chapter 552 of the Business and Commerce Code. It bans developing or deploying an AI system with intent to unlawfully discriminate, to manipulate behaviour, for social scoring, or to produce certain illegal content, and it requires government agencies to tell people when they are interacting with an AI system. The Attorney General has exclusive enforcement authority and the statute creates no private right of action.

decider.name: Office of the Attorney General of Texas

key_dates.note: HB 149 signed by the Governor
Chapter 552 took effect

public_access.how: Individuals can't sue under this chapter. The route is a complaint to the Attorney General, and a related statute requires the Attorney General to run an online AI complaint page. See item tx-2026-0010 for that page's statutory basis and for the verification gap on whether it exists yet.

title: Utilities Code limits how the PUCT may direct ERCOT, and bars verbal directives
summary: Texas law restricts the channels through which the Public Utility Commission may order ERCOT to act. A verbal directive is prohibited outright, and an official action may be directed only by contested case, by rulemaking, or by a written order or memorandum adopted on a majority vote. Separately, the ERCOT board selection committee, not the governor, picks ERCOT's directors and designates its chair.

key_dates.note: SB 2 (87R) added the board selection committee

public_access.how: Because a directive to ERCOT must run through a contested case, a rulemaking, or a majority vote taken in a meeting, each of those carries its own public participation route. PUCT open meetings are listed on the agency calendar feed and are open to the public in Commissioners Hearing Room 7-100.

claims.text: The commission may not verbally direct ERCOT and may direct official action only three ways.
claims.verbatim_quote: (a) The commission may not use a verbal directive to direct an independent organization certified under Section 39.151 to take an official action. The commission may direct the organization to take an official action only through: (1) a contested case; (2) rulemaking; or (3) a memorandum or written order adopted by a majority vote.
claims.source_title: Texas Utilities Code Sec. 39.1514, Commission Directives to Independent Organization

claims.text: The ERCOT board selection committee is three members, one each appointed by the governor, lieutenant governor and speaker.
claims.verbatim_quote: (a) The ERCOT board selection committee is composed of: (1) one member appointed by the governor; (2) one member appointed by the lieutenant governor; and (3) one member appointed by the speaker of the house of representatives.
claims.source_title: Texas Utilities Code Sec. 39.1513, ERCOT Board Selection Committee

claims.text: That committee selects ERCOT's governing body and designates its chair and vice chair.
claims.verbatim_quote: (d) The committee shall select members eligible under Section 39.151 to serve on the governing body of an independent organization certified under that section for the ERCOT power region and shall designate the chair and vice chair of the governing body from those members.
claims.source_title: Texas Utilities Code Sec. 39.1513, ERCOT Board Selection Committee

notes_for_editor: This item exists to give readers the legal frame for the August 3rd audit directive. It states what the statute says and stops there. It does NOT assert that the governor's directive was improper: the section binds the commission's directives to ERCOT, and a governor's letter to both agencies is a different instrument. Any characterisation beyond the quoted text needs a lawyer and a named source.

title: Texas Government Code Chapter 2054 carries three conflicting Subchapter S's on AI, with duplicated section numbers
summary: Three separate acts of the 89th Legislature each added a Subchapter S to Government Code Chapter 2054, and two of them number their sections identically. Section 2054.702 exists twice with entirely different commands, as do Sections 2054.701 and 2054.703 through 2054.705. The codifier has flagged the conflict in the published code rather than resolved it. Which text governs a state agency's AI duties is unsettled on the face of the statute.

key_dates.note: Both conflicting AI subchapters took effect

public_access.how: A codification conflict is resolved either by the Legislature in a future non substantive revision bill or by a court. There is no comment window. A reader who cares can raise it with their own legislator or with the Texas Legislative Council, which prepares the revision bills.

claims.verbatim_quote: Subchapter S, consisting of Secs. 2054.701 to 2054.713, was added by Acts 2025, 89th Leg., R.S., Ch. 1148 (S.B.  1964 ), Sec. 5. For another Subchapter S, consisting of Secs. 2054.651 to 2054.654, added by Acts 2025, 89th Leg., R.S., Ch. 951 (H.B.  5195 ), Sec. 1, see Sec. 2054.651 et seq., post. For another Subchapter S, consisting of Secs. 2054.701 to 2054.705, added by Acts 2025, 89th Leg., R.S., Ch. 1079 (H.B.  2818 ), Sec. 1, see Sec. 2054.701 et seq., post.
claims.source_title: Texas Government Code Chapter 2054, editorial note preceding Subchapter S

claims.text: One version of Section 2054.702 concerns generative AI technology.
claims.verbatim_quote: Sec. 2054.702. GENERATIVE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE TECHNOLOGY.
claims.source_title: Texas Government Code Sec. 2054.702, in the Subchapter S added by HB 2818

claims.text: The other version of Section 2054.702 requires a statewide AI code of ethics.
claims.verbatim_quote: Sec. 2054.702. ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE SYSTEM CODE OF ETHICS.  (a) The department by rule shall establish an artificial intelligence system code of ethics for use by state agencies and local governments that procure, develop, deploy, or use artificial intelligence systems.
claims.source_title: Texas Government Code Sec. 2054.702, in the Subchapter S added by SB 1964

claims.text: That code of ethics must align with a named federal framework.
claims.verbatim_quote: the artificial intelligence system code of ethics must include guidance for the deployment and use of artificial intelligence systems and heightened scrutiny artificial intelligence systems that aligns with the Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0) published by the National Institute of Standards and Technology.
claims.source_title: Texas Government Code Sec. 2054.702(b), in the Subchapter S added by SB 1964

claims.text: Local governments as well as state agencies must adopt the code of ethics.
claims.verbatim_quote: (c) State agencies and local governments shall adopt the code of ethics developed under this section.

notes_for_editor: Found by reading the code, not reported anywhere we saw, and it is the strongest original finding in this seed set. The conflict is real and is visible in the state's own published text. One caution for the write up: duplicate subchapter designations are a routine artefact of a busy session and are usually cleaned up in the next non substantive revision bill, so the honest framing is that the code currently carries a conflict, not that anyone did something wrong. Worth checking whether the 89th Legislature's later called sessions already fixed it.

title: DIR must run an AI regulatory sandbox letting state agencies test systems outside normal rules
summary: The Department of Information Resources is required to establish a programme letting eligible public entities contract with registered vendors to test AI systems before deployment, expressly without full compliance with otherwise applicable regulations. Vendors apply, and participants file quarterly reports. The department must report to the Legislature by November 30th of each even numbered year, which makes November 30th, 2026 the first reporting date.

key_dates.note: SB 1964 took effect
Department report to the Legislature due, per Sec. 2054.706(g)

public_access.how: The application process runs to vendors registered with DIR, not to the general public, and the statute provides no public comment step. The public visibility point is the report the department owes the Legislature by November 30th, 2026. A reader can ask DIR for the vendor application process and for any quarterly reports already filed.

claims.text: The sandbox is defined as testing without full regulatory compliance.
claims.verbatim_quote: "Program" means the program established by this section that is designed to allow temporary testing of an artificial intelligence system in a controlled, limited manner without requiring full compliance with otherwise applicable regulations.

notes_for_editor: Kept as its own item because it is the provision most likely to collide with the local data center fights elsewhere in this docket. title: Homeland Security tested facial biometric capture on pedestrians walking out of the country at the Progreso International Bridge
summary: The Department of Homeland Security Science and Technology Directorate brought industry partners to the Progreso International Bridge in Hidalgo County to demonstrate facial biometric image capture for U.S. Customs and Border Protection. Customs and Border Protection asked for the work in October 2025. Six companies were invited to the Maryland Test Facility in early 2026 for basic capability demonstrations. Three solutions were selected for further data collection. Two came from NEC National Security Systems and one was a joint solution from Paravision and AiFi. A replica of the pedestrian exit environment was built at the Maryland Test Facility first. The partners then arrived at Progreso in May. Cameras were mounted on poles at different heights. Testing ran after dark as well as in daylight with external lighting configurations. The partners used artificial intelligence to construct a three dimensional digital environment of the image capture zone. They also used it to observe pedestrian movement and to analyze whether facial images were suitable for matching in the Traveler Verification Service. Signs in English and Spanish told pedestrians that United States citizens could opt out. An opt-out lane was provided. The biometric entry and exit mandate applies to travelers who are not United States citizens. title: The state's checklist for a private school taking Education Freedom Account money has four requirements and none of them asks what teaches the child
summary: The Texas Education Freedom Accounts program publishes exactly four requirements a private school must meet to take state money on a student's behalf. It must be accredited, it must have run a campus for at least two years, it must administer a nationally norm referenced assessment, and it must be located in Texas or keep a Texas office if it is virtual. None of the four concerns curriculum, instructional method, or who or what delivers the teaching. The private school application period opened December 9th, 2025 and applications are taken on a rolling basis. Alpha School, which says on its own front page that an AI tutor gives students their coursework and that the adults in the room become Guides, names campuses in ten Texas cities.

title: The state technology agency publishes its account of carrying out the four AI laws the 89th Legislature passed
summary: The Texas Department of Information Resources published an account of its work implementing Senate Bill 1964, House Bill 2818, House Bill 3512 and House Bill 149.
